title: Cup with Handle
teaches: The cup with handle as we trade it: a leader that ran at least 30% rests in a smooth rounded U for seven weeks or more, climbs back near the old high, then dips into a quiet handle of five sessions or more that sits above the cup's midpoint, drifts down and holds the 50-day; the buy is the trade through the handle high at market in regular hours, the stop a few cents under the day's low and never past the handle low, the first sell a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the trail, and a loss taken at the stop is the plan working.

facts.quote: Cup-with-handle patterns are shaped like the silhouette of a tea cup viewed from the side.
facts.claim: IBD: a cup with handle is shaped like a tea cup seen from the side.

facts.quote: Cups should show smooth action on the left and right sides of the pattern.
facts.claim: IBD: both sides of a cup should be smooth.

facts.quote: There shouldn't be jagged edges or many wild weekly swings of 10% to 15% or more.
facts.claim: IBD: no jagged edges or many wild weekly swings of 10% to 15% or more.

facts.quote: V-shaped patterns are less reliable.
facts.claim: IBD: V-shaped patterns are less reliable.

facts.quote: The pattern's basic requirements start with a run up of at least 30% before the stock turns down into a consolidation.
facts.claim: IBD: the cup needs a run up of at least 30% before it.

facts.quote: A proper cup base needs to span a minimum of seven weeks, while a flat base can be as short as five weeks.
facts.claim: IBD: a cup spans at least seven weeks.

facts.quote: The base must be at least seven weeks long, including the handle.
facts.claim: IBD: at least seven weeks, the handle included.

facts.quote: They range from seven weeks to as long as 65 weeks in length, with many forming over three to six months.
facts.claim: IBD: cups run 7 to 65 weeks, many forming over three to six months.

facts.quote: The size of the decline, or correction, in a cup base should generally be between 12% and 33%.
facts.claim: IBD: a cup's decline is generally between 12% and 33%.

facts.quote: In bear markets, cups can run as deep as 50%.
facts.claim: IBD: in bear markets cups can run as deep as 50%.

facts.quote: to correct 1-1/2 to 2-1/2 times the market averages
facts.claim: IBD: a growth stock's cup corrects 1.5 to 2.5 times the market averages.

facts.quote: A proper handle forms in the upper half of a base and drifts slightly downward along its price lows.
facts.claim: IBD: a proper handle forms in the upper half and drifts slightly down along its lows.

facts.quote: In the handle, the midpoint of the handle's high and low marks should be above the midpoint of the high and low of the left side of the cup
facts.claim: IBD: the handle's midpoint sits above the cup's midpoint.

facts.quote: Handles that form too low present added risk of failure during breakouts.
facts.claim: IBD: handles that form too low fail more often.

facts.quote: Second, a handle should generally form above the 50-day or 10-week moving averages.
facts.claim: IBD: a handle generally forms above the 50-day line.

facts.quote: Handles must be at least five days long, and typically last for several weeks.
facts.claim: IBD: handles are at least five days long.

facts.quote: If it's shorter than five days, it's not a handle.
facts.claim: IBD: under five days it is not a handle.

facts.quote: Stocks with wedging handles have a higher failure rate and often are seen in late-stage bases
facts.claim: IBD: wedging handles fail more often and show up in late-stage bases.

facts.quote: Overeager handles that wedge upward tend to fail, while handles that drift lower foreshadow assertive action.
facts.claim: IBD: handles that wedge up tend to fail; handles that drift lower lead to strong moves.

facts.quote: A wedging handle with no shakeouts is a sign to steer clear.
facts.claim: IBD: a wedging handle with no shakeouts is a reason to stay away.

facts.quote: Volume should mostly ease until the breakout.
facts.claim: IBD: volume mostly eases until the breakout.

facts.quote: Volume should dry up, evidence that the weak holders are just about gone.
facts.claim: IBD: volume in the handle dries up as weak holders leave.

facts.quote: Handles should have areas of tight trading and days or weeks where volume contracts sharply.
facts.claim: IBD: handles show tight trading and sharp volume contraction.

facts.quote: The buy point is located by taking the highest price in the handle and adding 10 cents.
facts.claim: IBD's buy point is the handle's highest price plus 10 cents.

facts.quote: the rule says to sell all your shares of a stock if it falls 7% or 8% below the price at which you bought it.
facts.claim: IBD's general loss limit is 7% or 8% below the purchase price.

facts.quote: It's usually best to buy when a stock breaks out from a first-stage or second-stage base.
facts.claim: IBD: it is usually best to buy a first- or second-stage base.

facts.quote: Breakouts from late-stage bases will often blow up.
facts.claim: IBD: late-stage breakouts often blow up.

facts.quote: Once your stock has broken out, take most of your profits when they reach 20% to 25%.
facts.claim: IBD's general profit rule: take most profits at 20% to 25%.

facts.quote: The Cup & Handle is the corrective action after a powerful stock advance.
facts.claim: Zanger: the cup is the rest after a powerful advance.

facts.quote: The stock will sell off into the correction in a downward fashion for maybe 20 to 35 percent off the old high point.
facts.claim: Zanger: the cup falls maybe 20% to 35% off the old high.

facts.quote: The handle is generally about 5% below the old high point. A handle that is any lower is generally a defective stock and contains higher risk for failure.
facts.claim: Zanger: the handle sits about 5% below the old high; lower is riskier.

facts.quote: The time to buy the stock, is as it emerges into new highs at the top of the handle and not the old high point set some 8 to 12 weeks ago.
facts.claim: Zanger buys as it emerges into new highs at the top of the handle.

facts.quote: the best stocks with this formation are found at the beginning of a market move after a good market correction, and not during, or at the end of a major market advance.
facts.claim: Zanger: the best cups come at the start of a market move after a correction.

facts.quote: The cup should be U-shaped, not V-shaped, but allow variations.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: the cup is U-shaped, not V-shaped.

facts.quote: From 7 to 65 weeks (allow variations).
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a cup lasts 7 to 65 weeks.

facts.quote: 1 week minimum with no maximum, forming in the upper half of the cup.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: the handle lasts at least a week and forms in the upper half.

facts.quote: The handle low (point C) is a good place to put a stop. Raise the stop as price rises.
facts.claim: Bulkowski puts the stop at the handle low and raises it as price rises.

facts.quote: buy when price closes above the right cup rim
facts.claim: Bulkowski buys on a close above the right rim.

facts.quote: A V-shaped bottom would be considered too sharp of a reversal to qualify.
facts.claim: StockCharts: a V-shaped bottom is too sharp to qualify.

facts.quote: the handle should not extend into the lower half of the cup.
facts.claim: AAII: the handle should not reach into the lower half of the cup.

facts.quote: prices should have advanced at least 30% from the last intermediate low.
facts.claim: AAII: price should have advanced at least 30% from the last intermediate low.

facts.quote: Stop first (by default a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, F62); the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
facts.claim: A3: stop first, a few cents under the day's low; the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit, skip.

facts.quote: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule (B20).
facts.claim: A4: the stop is the exit; it only moves up, never wider; the gap rule is the one exception.

facts.quote: Shares = account × risk % ÷ (entry − stop), rounded down, then capped: the size is the SMALLER of the risk-based size and the position cap
facts.claim: A5: shares are account times risk percent, divided by entry minus stop, rounded down, then capped.

facts.quote: "I almost never take a loss greater than 3%": the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy (a loss on the position, not the account).
facts.claim: A13: the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.

facts.quote: The stop may move up to breakeven between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell.
facts.claim: Our stop may move up to breakeven between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell.

facts.quote: A gap against the stop: the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop.
facts.claim: B20: on a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop.

facts.quote: With a ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.
facts.claim: B20's ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.

facts.quote: No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report; hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.
facts.claim: B22: no new buys in the 3 days before a report; hold through one only if up 5R.

facts.quote: No chasing: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.
facts.claim: C28: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.

facts.quote: Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink (A5).
facts.claim: C28: chasing costs size, because the stop stays put and the distance grows.

facts.quote: Too stretched to buy: skip a long that is more than 10% above its 9 EMA.
facts.claim: We skip a long that is more than 10% above its 9 EMA: too stretched to buy.

facts.quote: Later sells are a judgment too: sell more into strength on a later push, and trail what is left.
facts.claim: Later sells are a judgment: sell more into strength on a later push, and trail what is left.

facts.quote: Default trail: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones; sell what is left on a close below it.
facts.claim: Our default trail: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones; a close below it sells what is left.

facts.quote: Entries are market orders.
facts.claim: E57: entries are market orders.

facts.quote: No new buys outside regular trading hours.
facts.claim: E58: no new buys outside regular hours.

facts.quote: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it.
facts.claim: F62: the stop sits a few cents under the day's low.

facts.quote: The market reading as a guide (A10): Green, full risk per grade and up to 10 positions; Yellow, smaller and fewer; Orange, only A+ setups; Red, mostly cash and shorts.
facts.claim: F65: Green full risk; Yellow smaller and fewer; Orange only A+; Red mostly cash and shorts.

facts.quote: After a market correction, when the reading turns Green again, start with a few positions and add more only as the first ones work
facts.claim: F68: after a correction, start with a few positions and add as they work.

facts.quote: After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule.
facts.claim: B21: after a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade.

facts.quote: Setup grades set the size: A and B setups at normal size; A+ sized up; B- or lower sized down.
facts.claim: D38: A and B normal size, A+ sized up, B- or lower sized down.

facts.quote: In a Red market: mostly cash, plus shorts below the 200-day.
facts.claim: D46: in a Red market, mostly cash plus shorts below the 200-day.

facts.quote: A climax run on your own long (Bracco's parabolic burst): sell a big part into it, a judgment call.
facts.claim: C34: sell a big part of a long into a climax run.

facts.quote: a 3-5 day final leg: three straight up days, two straight overnight gap ups, two of three days of range expansion, two days of rising volume, and a gap up on the climax day
facts.claim: B26: the parabolic burst is a 3 to 5 day final leg of up days, gaps, range expansion and rising volume.

facts.quote: Grading a setup (A+, A, B, B-) is discretionary and hard to define; no fixed checklist is taught as ours.
facts.claim: E50: grading is discretionary; no fixed checklist is ours.

facts.quote: The pivot is the highest price in the handle.
facts.claim: The pivot is the handle's highest price.

facts.quote: IBD adds 10 cents; with market orders the 10 cents does not matter.
facts.claim: IBD's 10 cents does not matter with a market order.

facts.quote: Price trades above the pivot during regular hours. Buy with a market order.
facts.claim: The trigger: price trades above the pivot in regular hours; buy at market.

facts.quote: The stock rose at least 30% from its lowest low of the prior 6 months (120 sessions) to the left-side high.
facts.claim: At least 30% from the lowest low of the prior 6 months to the left-side high.

facts.quote: At least 7 weeks (35 sessions) from the left-side high to the day before the breakout, the handle included.
facts.claim: At least 7 weeks, the handle included.

facts.quote: A rounded U, not a V: at least 30% of the cup's bars have their low in the cup's bottom quarter.
facts.claim: A rounded U: at least 30% of the cup's bars have lows in its bottom quarter.

facts.quote: At most two weeks inside the cup with a high-to-low range of 10% or more.
facts.claim: At most two weeks with a 10% or wider range inside the cup.

facts.quote: The right side climbs back to within about 10% of the left-side high before the handle starts.
facts.claim: The right side climbs back within about 10% of the left-side high before the handle.

facts.quote: The handle is at least 5 sessions long.
facts.claim: The handle is at least 5 sessions long.

facts.quote: The handle's midpoint (halfway between its high and low) sits above the cup's midpoint.
facts.claim: The handle's midpoint sits above the cup's midpoint.

facts.quote: The handle's lows drift sideways to down: a straight line fitted through the handle's daily lows slopes flat or down. Rising lows (a wedge) is not a handle.
facts.claim: The handle's lows drift sideways to down; rising lows are a wedge, not a handle.

facts.quote: The handle's average daily volume is below the cup's average daily volume.
facts.claim: The handle's volume averages below the cup's.

facts.quote: The handle holds above the 50-day line: no daily close below the 50-day SMA during the handle.
facts.claim: No daily close below the 50-day during the handle.

facts.quote: Tight at the end: the last 5 handle closes sit within about 3% of each other.
facts.claim: Tight at the end: the last 5 handle closes within about 3% of each other.

facts.quote: A few cents under the low of the buy day, or of the prior day.
facts.claim: The stop: a few cents under the buy day's low or the prior day's low.

facts.quote: Never wider than a few cents under the handle low: below the handle low the setup has failed. IBD's 7% to 8% loss limit is a reference, not ours.
facts.claim: Never wider than a few cents under the handle low; IBD's 7% to 8% is not ours.

facts.quote: 62% of cup breakouts come back to the breakout price within 30 days (Bulkowski). The day's-low stop will be tested often; that is normal, not a reason to widen it.
facts.claim: 62% of cup breakouts come back to the breakout price within 30 days; the stop is tested, not widened.

facts.quote: After the buy, a close back into the handle is a warning, not an exit by itself.
facts.claim: A close back into the handle is a warning, not an exit.

facts.quote: First or second base since the last real correction; a third or later base is graded down.
facts.claim: First or second base; a third or later is graded down.

facts.quote: Before the buy: the cup is a V, or deeper than 35% outside a bear market.
facts.claim: A V, or deeper than 35% outside a bear market, ends the setup.

facts.quote: Before the buy: the handle runs past about 6 weeks (30 sessions) with no breakout; the base is getting stale.
facts.claim: A handle past about 30 sessions with no breakout is stale.

facts.quote: Before the buy: volume rises through the handle.
facts.claim: Volume rising through the handle ends the setup.

facts.quote: Before the buy: a close below the 50-day during the handle.
facts.claim: A close below the 50-day during the handle ends the setup.

facts.quote: Before the buy: the handle's lows rise (wedging), or the handle is shorter than 5 days.
facts.claim: Rising handle lows, or a handle under 5 days, end the setup.

facts.quote: Up to 50% deep only for a cup formed in a bear market.
facts.claim: Up to 50% deep only in a bear market.

facts.quote: The cup falls no more than about 2.5 times the index's decline over the same weeks.
facts.claim: The cup falls no more than about 2.5 times the index's decline.

facts.quote: A cue, not a rule: best at the start of a new market uptrend after a correction, with the group leading and several of its stocks setting up.
facts.claim: Best at the start of a new uptrend, with the group leading.

facts.quote: A flat base falls 15% or less and stays boxy with a flat ceiling tapped at least twice; a cup falls 12% to 33% in a rounded U and then dips again into a handle before the buy.
facts.claim: A flat base stays boxy; a cup is a deeper rounded U followed by a handle.

facts.quote: A cup is one rounded decline whose right side climbs back within 10% of the old high, then one handle at the rim; a VCP shows two or more separate pullbacks, each smaller than the last
facts.claim: A cup is one rounded decline and one handle; a VCP is two or more shrinking pullbacks.

facts.quote: pauses 5 to 30 sessions with no rounded decline; a cup follows a 30% run and takes at least 7 weeks to round out and handle.
facts.claim: A high tight flag pauses with no rounded decline; a cup follows a 30% run and takes 7 weeks or more.

facts.quote: Calling a 2 or 3-day dip a handle; under 5 days it is not one.
facts.claim: A named mistake: calling a 2 or 3-day dip a handle.

facts.quote: Treating the measured-move target as a sure thing; Bulkowski found only 61% reach it.
facts.claim: A named mistake: treating the measured-move target as a sure thing.

facts.quote: ch.handle_volume: dries up sharply
facts.claim: The A+ handle volume dries up sharply.

facts.quote: ch.shape_no_wild_weeks: jagged, V-ish, two violent weeks inside (ULTA)
facts.claim: A jagged cup with violent weeks inside is a B- cue.

facts.quote: ch.base_count: third or later
facts.claim: A third or later base is a B- cue.

facts.quote: A handle in the upper third of the base, within about 5% of the old high, is better.
facts.claim: A handle in the upper third, within about 5% of the old high, is better.

facts.quote: Best between 3 and 6 months (63 to 126 sessions), symmetric; very long or lopsided cups grade down.
facts.claim: Cups are best between 3 and 6 months long.

facts.quote: A wedging or deep handle, a V-shaped cup or a late base breaks out and fades back through the pivot to the stop.
facts.claim: The failure mode: a bad handle, a V or a late base fades back through the pivot to the stop.

facts.quote: A very tight trigger-day stop is cheap but fragile; the house answer is the breakeven move at 2R to 5R (B19), not a wider stop.
facts.claim: BX: a very tight stop is fragile; the answer is breakeven at 2R to 5R, not a wider stop.

facts.quote: A cup over 6 months old with the handle resting on the 50-day is a late, tired base; the base-count rule is the filter the scan cannot apply.
facts.claim: WDAY: a cup over 6 months old with the handle on the 50-day is a late, tired base.

facts.quote: Before the buy: the market reading turns Red.
facts.claim: A Red reading before the buy ends the setup.

facts.quote: Never move the stop closer to make it fit.
facts.claim: Never move the stop closer to make the size fit.

facts.quote: ch.handle_position: just above the midpoint
facts.claim: A handle just above the cup's midpoint is a B- cue.

facts.quote: The cleanest of the ten: symmetric cup, quiet handle, breakout on 2.7x volume, 3R the next day.
facts.claim: FFIV: symmetric cup, quiet handle, 2.7x breakout, 3R the next day.

facts.claim: MCO: a handle almost a month long still works if its lows drift down, volume dries up and the 50-day holds; 3R in 4 sessions.
AX, trigger 2026-01-05: a 16.6-week, 20.2% cup after a 72% run; a 5-day handle; buy 89.22, stop 86.95; 1.48x volume; best 5.6R.

facts.quote: Handle volume barely below the cup's (0.97x): the grading cue at its weakest acceptable.
facts.claim: RRC: handle volume at 0.97x the cup's, the weakest acceptable.

facts.claim: ULTA: a mid-range close, a four-day fade to the stop, best 0.91R; a B- base.
BX, trigger 2019-11-26: buy 53.11, stop 52.49 (1.17%); stopped 4 sessions later at a low of 51.78.

facts.claim: BX: a 4.9x breakout reached 2.37R on day two, then one dip took the stop and the stock went on without us.

walkthroughs.title: FFIV, January 2014: the clean one
steps: FFIV ran 40%, then carved a cup, 15.6 weeks and 17.5% deep. Round at the bottom, a U, not a V.
Then a 7-day handle, 4.2% deep, up in the top half of the base. Volume dries up to 0.74 times the cup's.
January 13, 2014, it clears the handle high on 2.71 times volume. Buy at market, 91.29. Stop under the day's low, 90.67.
Fade back through the pivot and the idea's wrong. Instead, 3R the next day. As clean as they come.

walkthroughs.title: MCO, September 2012: the long handle
steps: Here's the slow version. MCO ran 40%, then spent 21.6 weeks building a cup 21.3% deep.
The handle drags on 19 days, 6.7% deep. But the lows drift down, volume dries up and it holds the 50-day.
September 6 it clears the handle high on 1.6 times volume. Buy at market, 40.76, stop under the day's low, 39.73.
A handle that wedges up or sinks too low, I pass. This one did neither, and hit 3R in 4 sessions.

walkthroughs.title: AX, January 2026: the sells and the trail
steps: AX ran 72%, then built a 16.6-week U, 20.2% deep. The handle is short, just 5 days, and that's enough.
January 5, 2026, it clears the handle high on 1.48 times volume. Buy at market, 89.22. Stop under the day's low, 86.95.
It grinds to 5R in about 7 weeks. Sell some into that push, and by now your stop sits at breakeven.
Then it rolls over under the pivot. A steady one trails the 20 EMA. A close under it sells the rest.

questions.q: You're flipping through charts and this one stops you. How would you describe what you're looking at?
choices: A rounded U, then a dip near the top
A tight box under a flat ceiling
Pullbacks that keep getting smaller
A short pause, no rounded decline

wrong.A tight box under a flat ceiling: That's a flat base. This one rounded down 14.6% and came back up, a U, not a box.
wrong.Pullbacks that keep getting smaller: That's a VCP, two or more pullbacks, each smaller than the last. Here it's one rounded decline and one dip.
wrong.A short pause, no rounded decline: That's a flag. This stock spent about 10 weeks rounding out before the dip.

questions.answer: A rounded U, then a dip near the top
questions.why: A rounded U, then a dip near the top. That's a cup with handle. The stock ran 31%, rounded down 14.6% and came all the way back over about 10 weeks. The handle is that last 7-day dip, on 0.66x the cup's volume. It's the final shakeout of weak holders, right under the old high. I want a U, not a V. A U means the stock spent time at the bottom while the sellers wore out.
questions.lesson_line: First the U, then the handle. A rounded rest after a run, then one last small dip under the high.
questions.simple: A rounded U after a strong run, then one small dip near the old high that shakes out the weak holders.

reasons: +1 fixed before (variety rewrite)

questions.story: A leader ran 31%, then spent about 10 weeks basing, 14.6% deep. It's back near the old high, and the last 7 days dipped on light volume.

deeper.example: IBD's picture of it: cup-with-handle patterns are shaped like the silhouette of a tea cup viewed from the side. Zanger calls the cup the corrective action after a powerful stock advance.

questions.q: You're writing tonight's plan. Where does the buy go?
choices: Through the handle's high
Through the old high before the cup
At the handle's low, before it turns
On a test of the cup's low

wrong.Through the old high before the cup: That old high is weeks back. The handle's high is the line the stock is pressing on now, so that's the trigger.
wrong.At the handle's low, before it turns: That's guessing the turn. Until it trades through the handle's high, the stock is still resting and can keep sliding.
wrong.On a test of the cup's low: Back at the cup's low the base has broken. We buy strength at the top, not a failed base at the bottom.

questions.why: Through the handle's high. That's the pivot, the highest price in the handle. The handle is where the last sellers near the old high get worked off. When price trades through its high, those sellers are used up and the stock is free to run. I buy that trade-through at market, in regular hours. Mark the level tonight and set an alert, so you buy the break and don't chase it an hour later.
questions.lesson_line: The handle's high is the trigger. Mark it the night before and let price come through it.
questions.simple: We buy as price trades through the handle's high, because until then the stock is still resting.

reasons: +2 rests on held decision D-003 (the 10 cents offset)
+1 fixed before (variety rewrite)

questions.story: Tomorrow this one could trigger. The stock ran 35%, built an 11-week cup, and has a 7-day handle sitting just under the old high.

deeper.counter: Zanger buys as it emerges into new highs at the top of the handle, not at the old high point. IBD adds 10 cents to the handle high. With a market order those cents don't matter.

questions.q: You buy a cup breakout at 91.29. The cup bottomed 17.5% below its old high. Your stop goes a few cents under the cup's low.
questions.why: False. Your stop goes a few cents under the low of the day, the LOD, or the prior day's low. On FFIV's breakout that was 90.67, just 0.7% under the 91.29 fill. A stop at the cup's low sits near the bottom of a 17.5% base. At 0.7% you can carry a real position. Down there, the same risk buys you a sliver, or the loss gets huge. I almost never take a loss over 3%. The low of the day is where the breakout is proven wrong.
questions.lesson_line: The stop lives under the low of the day, not at the bottom of the base.
questions.simple: False. The stop goes under the low of the day, because down at the cup's low the loss is far too big.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62)
+1 fixed before (variety rewrite)

questions.q: A sharp V-shaped drop and rebound still counts as a cup if the depth is right.
questions.why: False. A cup must be a rounded U, and a V fails even when the depth fits. IBD: V-shaped patterns are less reliable. StockCharts: a V-shaped bottom is too sharp of a reversal to qualify. Our card needs at least 30% of the cup's bars to have their low in the cup's bottom quarter.
questions.lesson_line: A cup is rounded. A V is a fast round trip, not a rest.
questions.simple: False. A V is too sharp and quick to be a cup, even when the depth is right.

deeper.trap: A V and a U can fall the same amount. The difference is time at the bottom. Our card wants at least 30% of the cup's bars to have lows in its bottom quarter. A V drops, turns and climbs straight back, so it spends too few bars down there.

reasons: stable definition, IBD and StockCharts agree

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A handle must last a minimum of ___ sessions to count as one.
questions.why: 5. A handle needs a minimum of 5 sessions. IBD: if it's shorter than five days, it's not a handle. IBD also says handles must be at least five days long.
questions.lesson_line: Five sessions or it is not a handle. Count them.
questions.simple: A handle needs a minimum of 5 sessions. Under five days it is not a handle.

reasons: stable definition, IBD states it twice

questions.q: Before you plan the buy, check where that dip sits. Where do you want a handle to form?
choices: Up in the top half of the base
Down near the cup's low
Right at the middle of the base
Under the 50-day line

wrong.Down near the cup's low: A dip back toward the cup's low gives up most of the base. That's no pause near the highs, and low handles fail more often.
wrong.Right at the middle of the base: Half of that handle would hang in the bottom half. We want the whole thing up top, its midpoint above the cup's.
wrong.Under the 50-day line: A handle should hold above the 50-day. Slipping under it means a bigger break in the trend, not a rest.

questions.answer: Up in the top half of the base
questions.why: Up in the top half, and this one is. A 4.6% dip right under the old high means buyers never let it slip. They held it near the highs while the last sellers cleared out. A handle that sags into the bottom half is a stock losing its grip, and those break out and fail more often. Here the handle's midpoint sits well above the cup's. That's what I want to see.
questions.lesson_line: The handle lives up top, near the old high. If it sags into the bottom half, I pass.
questions.simple: Up top. A handle near the old high shows buyers held the stock there, and low handles fail more often.

reasons: IBD, Bulkowski and AAII agree

questions.story: A 39% run, then a rounded 15-week cup, 17.5% deep. The last 6 days dipped 4.6%, right under the old high.

deeper.counter: IBD: handles that form too low present added risk of failure during breakouts. Zanger puts a good handle about 5% below the old high. AAII: the handle should not extend into the lower half of the cup.

questions.q: On this chart, volume has dried up through the handle compared with the cup.
questions.why: True. The handle ran 19 days at 0.77x the cup's average volume. That's volume drying up, and it means the sellers are mostly done. The people who wanted out near the old high already sold. With fewer shares for sale, it doesn't take much buying to push it through the handle's high. I like seeing it, and it raises the grade. It's not a must, though.
questions.lesson_line: Volume dries up in a good handle. The sellers are running out, and that raises the grade.
questions.simple: True. Volume dries up because the sellers are mostly done, so a little buying can push it through.

reasons: IBD and the card agree

deeper.example: IBD: volume should dry up, evidence that the weak holders are just about gone. Volume should mostly ease until the breakout.

questions.q: When do you actually pull the trigger?
choices: When it trades through the pivot
On a close above the pivot
Premarket, if it's already over
At the handle low, ahead of it

wrong.On a close above the pivot: That's a later entry. By the close you've often paid up, and with the same stop that means fewer shares.
wrong.Premarket, if it's already over: We don't buy outside regular hours. Let it open and trade through the pivot.
wrong.At the handle low, ahead of it: That's guessing the turn before the stock proves anything. The buy is the trade through the handle's high.

questions.answer: When it trades through the pivot
questions.why: When it trades through the pivot. Regular hours, market order, the moment price goes through the handle's high. That trade-through is the breakout. Buying right there keeps your fill close to the pivot and your stop close to your fill. Wait for the close and you're often paying up with the same stop under you, so fewer shares for the same risk. Premarket is out too. We don't buy outside regular hours.
questions.lesson_line: The trigger is the trade through the handle's high. Market order, regular hours, no waiting for the close.
questions.simple: We buy the moment it trades through the pivot in regular hours. Waiting for the close means paying more.

deeper.counter: Two published entries differ. Bulkowski buys when price closes above the right cup rim. Zanger buys as it emerges into new highs at the top of the handle, not at the old high point. We use the second kind of entry: the trade through the handle high, at market, in regular hours.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, E58)
+1 fixed before (variety rewrite)

questions.story: A 52% run, a 7.6-week cup, and a 6-day handle with volume drying up. The handle's high is your pivot. The open is minutes away.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The shortest a cup with handle can be is ___ weeks, the handle included.
questions.why: 7 weeks. IBD: the base must be at least seven weeks long, including the handle. Our card counts 35 sessions from the left-side high to the day before the breakout. Bulkowski's range starts at 7 weeks too.
questions.lesson_line: Seven weeks or more. A real cup takes time to build.
questions.simple: The shortest cup with handle is 7 weeks, and the handle counts toward that time.

reasons: IBD and Bulkowski agree

questions.q: A rounded U only counts as a cup when the stock had a strong run into it first.
questions.why: True. A cup is a leader resting after a big move. No run, nothing to rest from. Without it you're looking at a stock that dipped and came back, and that's not a leader. I want the stock that already proved it can move, then sat quiet while the weak holders left. That's the one that breaks out of the handle and runs again.
questions.lesson_line: No run, no cup. I want a leader resting, not a stock that just dipped.
questions.simple: True. A cup is a leader resting after a big run, so with no run first there's no leader to buy.

reasons: +1 fixed before (variety rewrite)

deeper.example: IBD and AAII both look for a run of at least 30% before the base. Zanger calls the cup the corrective action after a powerful stock advance.

questions.q: A handle's lows rise day after day into the pivot, with no shakeout. What kind of handle is that?
choices: A handle that wedges up
A handle that runs sideways
A handle that drifts down
A handle with a shakeout

wrong.A handle that drifts down: Drifting means the lows slope sideways to down. Rising lows are the opposite.
wrong.A handle that runs sideways: Sideways means the lows stay level. These lows rise day after day, which is a wedge.
wrong.A handle with a shakeout: The story says there is no shakeout here. The lows only climb.

questions.why: A handle that wedges up. IBD: a wedging handle with no shakeouts is a sign to steer clear. Overeager handles that wedge upward tend to fail, while handles that drift lower foreshadow assertive action. Our card says the handle's lows drift sideways to down, and rising lows are not a handle.
questions.lesson_line: A handle drifts down or sideways. Rising lows into the pivot are a wedge.
questions.simple: Rising lows with no shakeout make a wedging handle. IBD says steer clear, because wedging handles tend to fail.

deeper.trap: A wedge can look like strength, because the stock holds up and the lows climb. That is the trap. IBD reads it the other way: handles that wedge upward tend to fail, while handles that drift lower foreshadow assertive action.

reasons: IBD states it in two articles

questions.q: A good handle holds above the 50-day line while it drifts down.
questions.why: True. The handle is a short rest near the highs, and the 50-day is the trend under it. Holding above it says buyers are still defending the uptrend. A close under the 50-day during the handle is a different animal. That's a real crack in the trend, not a pause, and I'd want to see it repair before I get involved.
questions.lesson_line: The handle rests above the 50-day. A close under it is a crack, not a pause.
questions.simple: True. A handle is a short rest near the highs, and falling under the 50-day is a crack in the trend.

reasons: +2 the one-close test is a proposed card line, listed in the lesson conflicts

deeper.example: IBD: a handle should generally form above the 50-day or 10-week moving averages.

questions.q: How far below the left-side high may the right side stop before the handle starts, on our card?
choices: About 10% below it, at most
About 20% below, at most
About 30% below, at most
It must hit the old high

wrong.About 30% below, at most: Far too loose. A right side that stops well short leaves the handle low in the base, and low handles fail more.
wrong.It must hit the old high: Zanger puts the handle about 5% below the old high, so the right side does not have to reach it.
wrong.About 20% below, at most: Too loose. Our card wants the right side back within about 10% of the left-side high.

questions.why: About 10% below it, at most. Our card has the right side climb back to within about 10% of the left-side high before the handle starts. Only then can the handle sit high in the base. Zanger puts the handle about 5% below the old high and calls a lower one riskier.
questions.lesson_line: The right side comes back up near the old high. Only then does a handle start.
questions.simple: The right side should climb back to within about 10% of the left-side high before the handle starts.

reasons: +1 fixed before (why rewritten by the checker)

questions.q: Once a cup breaks out, it rarely comes back to the breakout price.
questions.why: False. Most of them come back. About 62% of cup breakouts trade back to the breakout price, so plan on it. When yours dips back to the pivot a few days later, that's normal. Don't widen the stop and don't panic sell. The stop under the low of the day decides if the trade is over, nothing else.
questions.lesson_line: Expect the retest. Most cup breakouts come back to the pivot, and the stop is still the decision.
questions.simple: False. Most cup breakouts come back to the breakout price, so a dip there is normal and the stop decides.

deeper.counter: Bulkowski's bull-market numbers show a 62% throwback rate. A pullback to the pivot is not a failure. The stop decides whether the trade is over.

reasons: +3 one cited fact only (Bulkowski)
+2 a measured statistic that Bulkowski updates
+1 fixed before (variety rewrite)

questions.q: What is the widest our cup stop can ever sit?
choices: 8% under the buy price
A few cents under the cup's low
Just under the handle low
Under the 200-day average

wrong.A few cents under the cup's low: That is the whole cup's depth away. Far too wide.
wrong.8% under the buy price: IBD's 7% to 8% is a reference, not ours.
wrong.Under the 200-day average: The 200-day decides whether we may buy a long at all, not where the stop sits.

questions.why: Just under the handle low, by a few cents. That is the outer wall. Below the handle low the setup has failed, so a wider stop is never allowed. The real stop usually sits much closer, a few cents under the day's low and within about 3% of the buy. Bulkowski also puts his stop at the handle low. IBD's 7% to 8% loss limit is a reference, not ours.
questions.lesson_line: The handle low is the outer wall. The real stop usually sits much closer.
questions.simple: The stop can never sit wider than a few cents under the handle low, because below it the setup has failed.

deeper.trap: The handle low is a limit, not a target. Pick the stop first: a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low. If that honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade. Never pull the stop closer to make the size fit, and never push it past the handle low to buy more room.

reasons: +2 the outer limit is a proposed card line (ch.stop_outer_limit)
+1 fixed before (variety rewrite)

questions.q: Late in a run, a third or fourth base is riskier to buy than a first or second one.
questions.why: True. The more bases a stock builds in one run, the more everyone already knows it. Early holders sit on big gains, ready to sell, and breakouts from late bases blow up more often. I still look at them. I just judge them less clean. A lower grade means I size down, not that I can't buy it.
questions.lesson_line: Count the bases. A late one gets a lower grade and a smaller size.
questions.simple: True. Late bases blow up more often, so I grade them lower and size down, but I can still buy them.

reasons: +2 rests on a proposed card line that conflicts with the SET.07 pilot (lesson conflicts)

deeper.example: IBD: it's usually best to buy when a stock breaks out from a first-stage or second-stage base. Breakouts from late-stage bases will often blow up.

questions.q: How many weeks with a 10% or wider range can a cup hold inside it, on our card?
choices: None at all
At most two
At most three
At most five

wrong.None at all: The card allows up to two. More than that is too jagged.
wrong.At most five: Five wild weeks is a jagged base. IBD wants smooth sides.
wrong.At most three: Three wild weeks is already too jagged. The card allows two.

questions.why: At most two. Our card allows at most two weeks inside the cup with a high-to-low range of 10% or more. IBD wants smooth action on both sides, with no jagged edges and not many wild weekly swings of 10% to 15% or more. A U shape alone is not enough, because smoothness is its own test.
questions.lesson_line: A cup is smooth. Count the violent weeks; more than two and it is not ours.
questions.simple: A cup can hold at most two weeks with a 10% or wider range. More wild weeks make it too jagged.

reasons: IBD and the card agree

questions.q: One R is what you risk per share, the fill minus the stop. What price is 3R?
questions.why: 43.17. Your risk is 40.98 minus 40.25 a share. Stack three of those on top of 40.98 and you land at 43.17. We count gains in R because it ties every win to what you risked to get it. A 3R winner made three times its risk, whatever the price. Don't treat 43.17 as an automatic sell, though. The first sell is a judgment, often into a 3, 5 or 7 day push.
questions.lesson_line: Know where 3R is before the open. It's a mark on the ruler, not an automatic sell.
questions.simple: Add three times your risk per share to the fill, which gives 43.17. R ties each gain to what you risked.

reasons: a computed key (38.60 + 3 x 0.70)
rests on the owner's rulebook B19: the hard rule is a third at 3R
the stem says hard rule because the owner's practice is to wait longer

wrong.$38.79: You took the three R off the fill instead of adding them. 3R sits above your buy.
wrong.$42.44: That's three R added to the stop, not the fill. Measure up from 40.98.
wrong.$41.71: That's one R above the fill. You need three.

questions.story: You bought the breakout at 40.98. Your stop sits a few cents under the low of the day, at 40.25. Now you mark your levels.

questions.q: Our card lets a cup fall up to about 2.5 times the index's decline over the same weeks.
questions.why: True. Our card says the cup falls no more than about 2.5 times the index's decline over the same weeks. IBD quotes O'Neil that growth stocks correct 1-1/2 to 2-1/2 times the market averages. So a leader falls more than the index, but not wildly more.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the cup against the market. A leader falls more than the index, but not wildly more.
questions.simple: True. A leader falls more than the index in a cup, but our card caps it at about 2.5 times.

reasons: the card and IBD agree

questions.q: IBD allows a cup to run as deep as 50% when it forms in a bear market.

questions.q: What do you do?

Widen the stop to the handle low
Sell now; the breakout has failed
Move the stop up to breakeven

questions.lesson_line: The retest is normal. The stop pays for it; you do not widen it.
questions.simple: Hold the stop where it is. Tests of the breakout price are normal, and the stop only moves up.

deeper.trap: Two moves feel safe and are wrong. Widening the stop breaks the rule that a stop never moves down or wider, and the gap rule is the only exception. Moving it to breakeven early skips the 2R to 5R window. A dip back to the pivot is a normal test, not a verdict.

Add, it's cheaper now

Plenty of cup breakouts come back to test the pivot and then go. Sell on a feeling and you throw away the ones that work. Dropping the stop or adding is how a small loss turns into a big one.
questions.lesson_line: A weak close is a warning. The stop is the decision.
questions.simple: Hold. The stop decides, and a close back in the handle is only a warning, since plenty of breakouts retest.

deeper.trap: Two reflexes follow a weak close: selling on feel, and adding because it's cheaper. The plan has neither. Wait for the stop. If it fills, take the loss and move on. Buy again only if it triggers again, as a new trade.

questions.q: Where's your stop now?

52.10, the first 30-minute low
No stop until it reclaims 52.94
Get out, the gap is past 2R

wrong.Get out, the gap is past 2R: Not here. At 52.10 the loss is still inside twice your risk, so the ceiling isn't hit.

If those 30 minutes push the loss past twice that, 2R, you're out. A stop at 52.10 keeps the loss inside 2R, so it stands.

questions.simple: The first 30-minute low becomes the new stop, so one panicky print doesn't decide. Past 2R, we get out.

deeper.trap: The gap rule is the only time a stop may move down. It is not 'no stop' and it is not 'sell at the open'. Wait for the first 30-minute bar and use its low as the new stop. Get out at once only if those 30 minutes take the loss past 2R.

A shallow cup with handle
A VCP of shrinking dips
Not a base at all

No, that's a V, not a U
No, 22% is too deep

Same grade, both are lighter
Neither, both fail on volume
