questions.lesson_line: Two checks at the fill: how far over the pivot, and how far over the 9 EMA.
questions.simple: Skip it. At 12% over the 9 EMA it's run away from support, and a normal pullback can stop you out.

deeper.trap: These are two separate checks. One: never buy more than 4% above the buy point. Two: skip a long that is more than 10% above its 9 EMA. Passing the first never excuses failing the second.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C28 and C29, both settled)

questions.q: On our card, is the cup still on your list?
questions.story: In week two of the handle the stock closes under its 50-day once. The next day it recovers above it.
choices: Yes; it recovered the next day
No; it closed under the 50-day
Yes; it takes two closes
No; the handle ran too long

wrong.Yes; it recovered the next day: The recovery does not undo the close. The card's test is one close.
wrong.Yes; it takes two closes: One close under the 50-day in the handle is enough.
wrong.No; the handle ran too long: A handle is usually 1 to 4 weeks, and week two is normal. Length is not the problem.

questions.why: No. On our card, one daily close below the 50-day during the handle ends the setup before the buy, and a recovery the next day does not undo it. IBD says a handle should generally form above the 50-day, and our card turns that into a one-close test. One close is enough, not two.
questions.lesson_line: Inside the handle the 50-day holds every close. One close under and I cross it off.
questions.simple: On our card, one close under the 50-day during the handle ends the setup, even if it bounces back the next day.

reasons: the one-close test is our card's own proposal, while IBD says only 'generally'

questions.q: On our card, a handle is tight at the end when its last 5 closes sit within about 3% of each other.
questions.why: True. Tight at the end means the last 5 handle closes sit within about 3% of each other. IBD asks for areas of tight trading in a handle, and the card gives one way to measure that.
questions.lesson_line: Tight closes into the pivot. That is the picture I want.
questions.simple: True. Our card calls a handle tight when its last 5 closes sit within about 3% of each other.

reasons: a proposed card row, with IBD agreeing on the idea of tight trading

questions.q: Both pass. Which one would you grade higher?
questions.story: Two clean cups. Both handles sit in the top half of the base. One is within 5% of the old high. The other sits just above the middle.
choices: The one near the old high
The one just above the middle
Same grade, both are up top
Neither, both sit too low

wrong.The one just above the middle: It passes, but it gave back more. Lower in the base carries more risk of failure.
wrong.Same grade, both are up top: Both pass, but where the handle sits still feeds the grade. Higher is cleaner.
wrong.Neither, both sit too low: Both sit in the top half, and one is within 5% of the high. Neither is too low.

questions.answer: The one near the old high
questions.why: The one near the old high. Both handles are in the top half, so both count. But a handle within 5% of the high means buyers barely let it slip. They held it right under the ceiling while the last sellers left. The one just over the middle gave back more, closer to where handles start to fail. I'd grade the higher one cleaner and give it more size.
questions.lesson_line: Higher in the base is cleaner. A handle held near the old high gets the better grade.
questions.simple: The one near the old high. Buyers held it right under the ceiling, so it's cleaner and grades higher.

reasons: the grade cues are proposed card rows, and the E50 rulebook line says grading is a judgment

deeper.counter: Zanger: the handle is generally about 5% below the old high point. A handle that is any lower contains higher risk for failure.

questions.q: You want this on your list tonight. What do you label it?
questions.story: A leader ran 72%, then fell 20.2% in a rounded U over 16.6 weeks. It climbed back near its high, then drifted down 4.9% for 5 days.
choices: A cup with a handle at the rim
A flat base ending in a dip
A VCP of shrinking dips
A high tight flag

wrong.A flat base ending in a dip: A flat base is a shallow box. 20.2% deep and rounded is a cup.
wrong.A VCP of shrinking dips: A VCP is two or more pullbacks, each smaller. This is one rounded decline and one handle.
wrong.A high tight flag: A flag pauses after the run with no rounded decline. This one spent 16.6 weeks rounding out.

questions.answer: A cup with a handle at the rim
questions.why: A cup with handle. It ran 72%, then rounded down 20.2% over 16.6 weeks. That's a real U, too deep and too round for a flat base. It came back near the high and dipped 4.9% for 5 days. One dip at the rim, not a string of smaller ones. The label matters because it gives you the plan. Buy the trade through the handle's high, stop under the low of the day.
questions.lesson_line: Depth and shape first. A deep rounded rest with one dip at the rim is a cup.
questions.simple: A deep rounded U with one small dip at the rim is a cup with handle. The plan is the trade through its high.

deeper.trap: Two clues sort most look-alikes. Depth and shape: a box is shallow, and a cup is a deeper rounded U. Pullbacks: a cup is one rounded decline and one handle, and a VCP is two or more that shrink. Check both before you name the base.

reasons: touches the held cup-depth band (D-052); 21% sits inside every option so no key depends on it

questions.q: Which one is the cup?
questions.story: Base A falls in one smooth curve, climbs back to the rim, then dips once. Base B: three pullbacks of 18%, 9% and 4%.
choices: Base A; one rounded decline
Base B; its first drop is 18%
Both; each ends in a small dip
Neither; both are plain VCPs

wrong.Base B; its first drop is 18%: Three pullbacks, each smaller than the last, is a VCP.
wrong.Both; each ends in a small dip: Only one has a single rounded decline and a handle.
wrong.Neither; both are plain VCPs: Base A is one rounded decline, a climb back to the rim and one small dip. That is a cup, not a VCP.

questions.why: Base A. A cup is one rounded decline whose right side climbs back near the old high, then one handle. Base B has three separate pullbacks of 18%, 9% and 4%, each smaller than the last. That is a VCP, not a cup.
questions.lesson_line: Count the pullbacks. One rounded decline and a handle is a cup; shrinking swings are a VCP.
questions.simple: A cup is one rounded decline and one handle, while Base B shows three shrinking pullbacks, which is a VCP.

deeper.trap: A cup's handle is also a small dip after a big one, so a cup can look like two shrinking pullbacks. The tell is the first one. A cup has one rounded decline whose right side climbs back near the old high. A VCP has separate swings, each smaller than the last.

reasons: card text for the cup and the VCP agree word for word

questions.q: A friend calls this a cup with handle. What is it really?
questions.story: The stock rose 120% in seven weeks. Then it paused sixteen sessions, 10% deep, just under the high.
choices: A cup with a handle at the rim
A high tight flag after a run
A flat base with a flat ceiling
A VCP of shrinking pullbacks

wrong.A cup with a handle at the rim: A cup takes many weeks to round out. This paused only sixteen sessions with no U.
wrong.A flat base with a flat ceiling: A flat base is a longer, calmer rest. Here you've got a short pause after a huge run.
wrong.A VCP of shrinking pullbacks: A VCP shows two or more pullbacks, each smaller. This is one tight pause.

questions.answer: A high tight flag after a run
questions.why: A high tight flag. 120% in seven weeks is a monster run, and sixteen sessions is a short pause right under the high. A cup needs weeks to round down and come back. This never rounded at all. It went sideways and tight after the run. That's a flag, the strongest kind, and you'd plan it like one.
questions.lesson_line: A huge run and a short pause is a flag. A long rounded rest is a cup.
questions.simple: A big run and a short tight pause is a flag. A cup needs many weeks to round out.

deeper.trap: A cup follows a strong run, and this run is far bigger. Do not stop at the run. A cup also takes many weeks to round out, and a sixteen-session pause has no time to build one. Ask whether it rounded, or only paused.

reasons: the high tight flag pole and flag length are pending owner decisions; the story uses a 120% pole and a sixteen-session pause, inside every held option
two card rows (the cup and the high tight flag) separate the cases

questions.q: It took your stop. Was that loss a mistake?
questions.story: A 16-week, 19% cup after a 76% run, then an 8-day handle. You bought the trigger at 260.96, stop 257.75. It closed mid-range, then faded four days into your stop.
choices: No, the stop did its job
Yes, the stop needed room
Yes, sell weak closes
No, so buy it back now

wrong.Yes, the stop needed room: The stop only moves up. More room just means a bigger loss on the ones that fail.
wrong.Yes, sell weak closes: A weak close is a warning. The stop is the exit, and selling on feel cuts the winners too.
wrong.No, so buy it back now: Buy again only if it triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop.

questions.answer: No, the stop did its job
questions.why: No. You bought 260.96 with the stop at 257.75, about 1.23% of risk. It faded four days and took the stop. That's the plan working, a small loss you picked before you bought. Judge the decision, not the result. Real trigger, honest stop, right size. That's a good trade even when it loses. The mid-range close was a warning, not an exit. Buy it again only on a new trigger.
questions.lesson_line: A loss at the stop is the system working. Judge the decision, not the result.
questions.simple: No. The stop capped a small loss you planned before the buy, so that's the plan working.

deeper.trap: A stop-out doesn't prove the setup was bad, and a winner doesn't prove it was good. Judge the decision: a real trigger, an honest stop, a size that fits the risk. After a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger.

reasons: story built from the unreviewed dossier example d20 and d21 (D-007)
the base grade is left out of the key and the explanation, since the story does not give it

questions.q: What do you do now?
questions.story: A 10-week, 18% cup with a 5-day handle breaks out on 4.9x volume. You bought 53.11, stop 52.49. On day two it reaches 2.37R.
choices: Widen the stop to give it room
Move the stop up to breakeven
Sell everything at 2.37R
Add shares while it's strong

wrong.Widen the stop to give it room: Never wider. A tight stop gets protected with breakeven, not by moving it down.
wrong.Sell everything at 2.37R: Too early. We rarely sell before day 3, and then it's part, into a push.
wrong.Add shares while it's strong: Adding to a winner is rare for us, a feel call, never the plan. The plan on day two is protecting the trade.

questions.answer: Move the stop up to breakeven
questions.why: Move the stop up to breakeven. Your stop was only 1.2% away, cheap but fragile. One normal dip can tag it. We can move the stop to breakeven anywhere from 2R to 5R, and 2.37R is inside that. It's your call, but I like it here. Now the trade can't turn into a loss. That's what happened on this one: a dip took the 1.2% stop, then the stock went on without us. Breakeven turns that into a scratch.
questions.lesson_line: A tight stop is cheap but fragile. Past 2R, breakeven protects it. Wider never does.
questions.simple: Move the stop to breakeven. Past 2R a winner shouldn't turn into a loss, and a tight stop is fragile.

deeper.trap: A tight stop gets hit by normal noise, and the urge is to widen it. The answer runs the other way. The stop may move up to breakeven from 2R, and it never moves wider. In BX the trade reached 2.37R on its second session. Then one dip took out the 1.2% stop, and the stock went on without us.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, breakeven between 2R and 5R, 'ideally')
story built from the unreviewed dossier example d22 and d23 (D-007)

questions.q: Next morning it trades under your stop. What do you do?
questions.story: A 30-week, 23% cup; the 8-day handle rests on the 50-day. You bought 273.63, stop 266.70. The day closed 270.71, low in its range.
choices: Out at the stop, as planned
Hold; the cup is still valid
Lower the stop under the handle

wrong.Hold; the cup is still valid: The stop is the exit. The cup's shape does not move it.
wrong.Lower the stop under the handle: The stop only moves up, never down.

questions.answer: Out at the stop, as planned
questions.why: Out at the stop, as planned. A cup over 6 months old with the handle resting on the 50-day is a late, tired base. If it sets up again, that is a new trade.
questions.lesson_line: Out at the stop. A new trigger later is a new trade with its own stop.

questions.q: Did you break a rule?
questions.story: The pivot is 72.58. It gaps open and you fill at 74.57. It never trades above your fill, and the next day takes the 73.36 stop.
choices: Yes, never buy a gap open
No, the fill was inside 4%
Yes, the stop was too tight
No, anything under 10% is fine

wrong.Yes, never buy a gap open: No rule bans a gap fill. Inside 4% of the pivot, it's a normal buy.
wrong.Yes, the stop was too tight: A tight stop under the low of the day isn't a rule break. It kept the loss small.
wrong.No, anything under 10% is fine: The chase line is 4% over the pivot. The 10% line is about the 9 EMA, a different check.

questions.why: No. The pivot was 72.58 and you filled at 74.57, 2.7% over it. That's inside our 4% chase line, so it's allowed. The stop at 73.36 did its job, and the loss was the plan. The tell was the gap that couldn't build. It never traded above your fill, and the next day it went through the stop. A gap that can't add to its open is a warning, not a broken rule.
questions.lesson_line: A fill inside 4% is allowed. A gap that can't build is the warning.
questions.simple: No rule was broken. The fill was inside 4%, and the stop kept the loss small, as planned.

deeper.trap: SCHW gapped over the 72.58 pivot at the open and filled 2.7% above it. It closed near its high, then fell through the stop the next day without ever trading above the fill. The fill was inside the 4% line and the stop was honored, so the loss was the plan.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C28 no-chase line)
story built from the unreviewed dossier example d26 and d27 (D-007)

questions.q: On a cup breakout, we give the stock IBD's full 7% to 8% before we sell.
questions.why: False. That's IBD's general loss limit, not ours. I almost never take a loss bigger than 3% on a position. Our stop goes a few cents under the low of the day or the prior day's low. That's where the breakout is proven wrong. On a good breakout that's close to your fill. Give every cup 7% to 8% and each loser costs you two or three times what it should.
questions.lesson_line: Our stop comes from the chart, under the low of the day. Not a fixed 7% or 8%.
questions.simple: False. I almost never lose more than 3%, so the stop goes under the low of the day, not at 7% to 8%.

deeper.trap: A flat percent loss limit is a different system. Ours starts from the chart. Stop first, a few cents under the low of the day, then the size comes from the stop. If the honest stop doesn't fit the risk, skip the trade. Never move the stop closer to make it fit.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3 and A13, the stop and its usual width)

questions.q: What do you do with the rest?
questions.story: A steady mover: you bought 89.22 with the stop at 86.95. You sold pieces into pushes on the way up. Weeks later it rolls over and closes under its trail line.
choices: Hold until it closes under the pivot
Sell it, the trail just broke
Hold, the stop is at breakeven
Buy more on the dip

wrong.Hold until it closes under the pivot: The pivot is way back at the start of the trade. Waiting for it gives back most of the move.
wrong.Hold, the stop is at breakeven: Breakeven guards against a loss. The trail is what sells the rest.
wrong.Buy more on the dip: The trend just broke. From here the plan only sells.

questions.answer: Sell it, the trail just broke
questions.why: Sell it. After the early sells, what's left rides a rising average. That's the 20 EMA for a steady mover like this one, the 9 EMA for a fast one. A close under it is your exit. The trail lets a winner run as long as the trend holds. This one hit 5R in about 7 weeks, then rolled over all the way back under the pivot. The trail had you out with most of the gain.
questions.lesson_line: Sell some into strength, trail the rest. The close under the line is the exit.
questions.simple: Sell it. A close under the trail line means the trend broke, and selling keeps most of the gain.

deeper.example: Bought at 89.22 with the stop at 86.95, it reached 5R in about 7 weeks, then rolled over below the pivot. That's what a trail is built for. A faster mover would ride the 9 EMA instead.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E51 and E52)
story built from the unreviewed dossier example d06 and d07 (D-007)

questions.q: Write the plan. Where's the stop, and how do you take your first profit?
questions.story: A 7-day handle. Price clears the handle high and you fill at 64.30. The lower of that day's and the prior day's low is 63.78.
choices: Just under 63.78, sell into a push
Right on 63.78, a third at 2R
Handle low, all of it at 5R
7% under the fill, half at 3R

wrong.Right on 63.78, a third at 2R: The stop goes a few cents under the low, not on it. And the first sell is a judgment, not a fixed 2R.
wrong.Handle low, all of it at 5R: The low of the day is the stop, closer than the handle low. And we sell in pieces, not all at once.
wrong.7% under the fill, half at 3R: 7% is IBD's loss limit, not ours. The stop goes just under the low of the day.

questions.answer: Just under 63.78, sell into a push
questions.why: A few cents under 63.78, and the first sell goes into a push. That low is where the buy is proven wrong. The stop sits just under it, never on it, so a normal tag doesn't take you out. The first sell is a judgment. I rarely sell before day 3, and I like selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push. Write all of it down before the open: entry, stop, size, and how you'll sell.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop, size and how you'll sell. Write it down before the open.
questions.simple: The stop goes just under 63.78, where the idea fails. The first sell is a judgment, into a strong push.

deeper.example: The stop is set first, and the sell plan follows. If it opens above a level where you planned to sell, selling part at the open is a judgment, never a rule.

reasons: the stop is computed from the story (90.72 less a few cents)
rests on the owner's rulebook (F62 and B19)
story built from the unreviewed dossier example d01 (D-007)

questions.q: Judging the handle, is this one you'd buy on the trigger?
choices: Yes, it's high and volume dried up
No, the handle sits too low
No, the handle wedges up
Yes, heavy volume shows demand

wrong.No, the handle sits too low: It sits right under the old high, well above the cup's midpoint.
wrong.No, the handle wedges up: Its lows drift down. A wedge has rising lows.
wrong.Yes, heavy volume shows demand: A handle should dry up, and this one did, at 0.74x. Heavy handle volume is a warning.

questions.answer: Yes, it's high and volume dried up
questions.why: Yes, that's one I'd want. The handle sits right under the old high and its lows drift down instead of climbing. Volume dried up to 0.74x the cup's. Buyers held it near the highs while the sellers ran out. That's the picture. The next day it cleared the handle's high on 2.71x volume. A great picture still isn't a promise, so the stop under the low of the day stays in.
questions.lesson_line: High in the base, lows drifting down, volume dried up. That's the picture. The stop still decides.
questions.simple: Yes. The handle sits high, its lows drift down and volume dried up, so the sellers are done.

deeper.trap: Judge the setup the day before, not on the breakout day. The handle already showed what mattered: high in the base, lows not rising, volume dried up. Rising volume through a handle is a warning.

reasons: chart item built from the unreviewed dossier example d01 and d02 (D-007)
fixed before (the question once gave away its own answer)

questions.story: A 40% run, a rounded cup, and a 7-day handle sitting just under the old high. Tomorrow it could trigger.

questions.q: Check the handle's lows. Do you buy the trigger?
choices: Yes, the cup is 20% deep
No, the handle's lows rise
Yes, it's right near the highs
No, the cup is too short

wrong.Yes, the cup is 20% deep: The cup is fine. The handle is the problem, its lows climb into the pivot.
wrong.Yes, it's right near the highs: Near the highs is the right place. The rising lows are what's wrong.
wrong.No, the cup is too short: 13 weeks is plenty for a cup. Pass for the handle, not the cup.

questions.why: No, I pass. Six days of higher lows into the pivot is a wedge, not a handle. A good handle drifts sideways to down and shakes out the weak holders. A wedge never does. Everyone who bought the climb is still in, and they sell the first pop. The 13-week, 20% cup is fine. The handle is the problem. This one never traded green, a best of 0.0R before the stop.
questions.lesson_line: The cup can be fine and the handle still wrong. Rising lows, I pass.
questions.simple: No. Rising lows into the pivot make a wedge with no shakeout, and wedges fail more often.

deeper.counter: IBD: handles that drift lower foreshadow assertive action, and overeager handles that wedge upward tend to fail. Most successful handles feature a shakeout, where prior lows in the handle are undercut.

reasons: chart item built from the unreviewed dossier example d30 (D-007)
fixed before (the 0.0R wording was reworded)

questions.story: A 13-week cup, 20% deep, and a clean climb back to the old high. It's spent six days building a handle right under the pivot.

questions.q: What do you do with the breakout?
questions.story: Your best cup is an A+, our cleanest grade. It sits a few cents under the pivot, above its 200-day. Overnight our market filter in the app flips to Red.
choices: Buy it, an A+ trades anywhere
No new long, mostly cash
Buy half size, tight stop
Skip it and short the stock

wrong.Buy half size, tight stop: Half size is still a new long into a market that's selling everything.
wrong.Buy it, an A+ trades anywhere: In Orange the A+ still gets money. Red is mostly cash, so this isn't the time to press.
wrong.Skip it and short the stock: We only short below the 200-day, and this stock is above it.

questions.why: No new long. At Red our filter is saying the market isn't backing breakouts, and in Red we sit mostly in cash. The reading is a guide, not a law, but Red is its loudest call. In Red even great cups break out into a market that's selling everything, and they get run over. Your A+ will still be there, or a better one, when it turns. Sit on your hands.
questions.lesson_line: Red means mostly cash. However good the cup looks, the market comes first.
questions.simple: No new long. In Red even a clean breakout is fighting the market, so we sit mostly in cash.

deeper.trap: The trap is the A+ exception. In Orange only A+ setups trade, so a great cup feels like an exception in Red. It isn't. Green is full risk, Yellow smaller and fewer, Orange only A+, Red mostly cash and shorts.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D46 and F65, the market reading as a guide)

questions.q: How many do you buy on day one?
questions.story: A correction just ended and our market filter turned Green, full risk, up to 10 positions. Six leaders in one group sit at their cup pivots.
choices: Most of them, Green is full risk
A few first, more as they work
None, wait a month to be sure
All six at half size

wrong.Most of them, Green is full risk: Green allows full risk, but after a correction you start with a few and let them prove it.
wrong.None, wait a month to be sure: This is when the best cups show up. Start small, don't sit out.
wrong.All six at half size: Half size on all six is still six positions on one unproven day.

questions.answer: A few first, more as they work
questions.why: A few first, more as they work. The first Green day after a correction can be a head fake. Buy all six, the turn fails, and six stops hit at once. Start with a few. If they work, the market's telling you the turn is real, and you buy the next ones. If they fail, you lost a little and you're mostly in cash. Let the market earn your exposure.
questions.lesson_line: Green after a correction: a few first. Let the winners earn the next ones.
questions.simple: A few first, more as they work. A new uptrend can be a head fake, so let it prove itself.

deeper.example: Zanger: the best stocks with this formation are found at the beginning of a market move after a good market correction.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F68, a few positions first after a correction)

questions.q: Can you hold it through the report?
questions.story: You bought a cup breakout at 50.00 with the stop at 48.00. It closes today at 61.20, and it reports tomorrow after the close.
choices: Yes, it's past the hold line
Yes, and add before the report
No, sell it before the report
No, it needs a bigger gain

wrong.Yes, and add before the report: Hold, yes. Add, no. We take no new buys in the 3 days before a report.
wrong.No, sell it before the report: Up more than 5R, you've earned the right to hold through it.
wrong.No, it needs a bigger gain: The line is 5R, and this trade is past it.

questions.answer: Yes, it's past the hold line
questions.why: Yes. Your risk was 50.00 minus 48.00 a share. You're up 61.20 minus 50.00, more than five times that. We hold through a report only when the trade is up 5R, and this one is. The reason is the gap. A stop can't catch an overnight gap, so you need a big cushion before you sit through one. Up 5R, a bad gap still leaves you a winner. Just don't add. No new buys in the 3 days before a report.
questions.lesson_line: Up 5R or more, you can hold through the report. Below that, you're out before it.
questions.simple: Yes. It's up more than five times its risk, enough cushion to sit through a gap, but don't add.

deeper.trap: The 5R line is about a trade already open. It doesn't let you add. Earnings are tomorrow, so you're inside the 3 days before a report and no new buys are allowed.

reasons: cites only one fact
rests on the owner's rulebook B22 (hold only if up 5R), which the story states because no earlier item teaches it

questions.q: If it works, how do you take your profits?
choices: At the cup's measured-move target
Most of it at a 20% to 25% gain
Into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, then trail
All of it back at the old high

wrong.At the cup's measured-move target: A target is a guess. Plenty of cups never reach it, and the best ones blow right past it.
wrong.Most of it at a 20% to 25% gain: That's IBD's rule, not ours. We sell into strength by judgment, then trail.
wrong.All of it back at the old high: The old high is right by the pivot. That's where the trade starts, not where it ends.

questions.answer: Into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, then trail
questions.why: Into a push, then trail the rest. I very rarely sell on day 1. I wait for strength, often a 3, 5 or 7 day push, and sell part into it. That banks real money while buyers are paying up. What's left rides the 9 EMA or the 20 EMA until it closes under. A fixed target caps your best trades, and the few big ones pay for everything.
questions.lesson_line: Sell some into strength and trail the rest. Targets are guesses.
questions.simple: Sell part into a strong push of a few days, then trail the rest so the winner can keep running.

deeper.counter: IBD says take most profits at 20% to 25%. Bulkowski found only 61% of cups reach the measured-move target. Our first sell is a judgment, often into a 3, 5 or 7 day push.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19 and E51)
the 20% to 25% and 61% figures are web numbers that can change

questions.story: The day before this one triggers. You're writing the plan, and that includes how you'll take profits.

questions.q: A handle that has run 12 sessions with no breakout is stale on our card.
questions.why: False. On our card a handle goes stale only after it runs past about 6 weeks, 30 sessions, with no breakout. At 12 sessions this one is still young. A dip shorter than five days is not a handle at all.
questions.lesson_line: A handle is a short pause. Past about 30 sessions with no breakout, it is a stall.
questions.simple: A handle at 12 sessions is not stale. Stale means past about 30 sessions with no breakout.

deeper.trap: Two different checks sit close together. Under 5 sessions the dip is not yet a handle, so there is nothing to call stale. Past about 30 sessions with no breakout the base is stale and the card takes it off. Young and old both mean no buy, but for different reasons.

reasons: the 30-session limit is a card proposal, a number that may be tuned
one card fact carries the key

questions.q: Take it?
questions.story: In a rising market, a leader's cup fell 42% in a rounded U. Then a tidy 8-day handle formed near the high.
choices: Take it; 8-day handle is tidy
Pass; the cup is too deep to count
Take it; IBD allows cups to 50%
Pass; an 8-day handle is short

wrong.Take it; 8-day handle is tidy: The handle passes. The cup is far too deep.
wrong.Take it; IBD allows cups to 50%: Only in a bear market. Here the market is rising.
wrong.Pass; an 8-day handle is short: Eight sessions clears the handle minimum of 5. The cup depth is what fails.

questions.answer: Pass; the cup is too deep to count
questions.why: Pass. On our card, a cup deeper than 35% outside a bear market ends the setup. This one fell 42% in a rising market. IBD says cups can run as deep as 50% in bear markets. Zanger puts cups at maybe 20% to 35% off the old high. A tidy handle does not fix a cup that fell too far.
questions.lesson_line: A tidy handle does not fix a cup that fell too far.
questions.simple: The cup fell 42%, deeper than 35%, and that is too deep outside a bear market. A tidy handle cannot fix it.

deeper.trap: Two traps. First, quoting IBD's 50% without its condition: that depth is for cups formed in a bear market. Second, letting a tidy handle rescue a deep cup. Check the market first, then the depth, and only then the handle.

reasons: rests on the held cup-depth decision D-052
a depth threshold that is a card proposal and can change

questions.q: Which one is never allowed?
questions.story: The breakout fills at 48.60. The buy day's low sits at 46.40, about 4.5% under your fill.
choices: Skip the trade; the stop is wide
Pull the stop in to 3% to fit
Wait for a tighter spot
Put the stop under the 46.40 low

wrong.Skip the trade; the stop is wide: Skipping is always allowed when the honest stop does not fit.
wrong.Wait for a tighter spot: Waiting is always allowed. No rule makes you buy this breakout. Pulling the stop in is not allowed.
wrong.Put the stop under the 46.40 low: Allowed, and it is the default: stop first, a few cents under the day's low. About 3% is only where the stop usually sits.

questions.answer: Pull the stop in to 3% to fit
questions.why: Pulling the stop in to 3% to fit is never allowed. Stop first, a few cents under the day's low. The size comes from the stop. If the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade. Never move the stop closer to make it fit.
questions.lesson_line: You never pick a size and back-fit a stop inside the noise.
questions.simple: Moving the stop closer just to make the size fit is never allowed. The stop comes first and the size follows from it.

deeper.trap: Do not treat 3% as a rule that sets the stop. The rulebook says the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy, because that is where the day's low usually falls. Start from the honest stop, never from a percent you want.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook A3 and A4
wrong note fixed before in the cold check

questions.q: It's your position. What do you do?
questions.story: Weeks after the breakout, your cup winner posts three up days in a row. The last two gap up overnight. Range widens on two of the three days, and volume rises on two days.
choices: Sell a big part into the run
Add, it's breaking out again
Nothing, let the trail decide
Sell a small slice, hold the rest

wrong.Sell a small slice, hold the rest: A climax gets a big part sold, not a slice. How big is your call.
wrong.Add, it's breaking out again: A burst is the end of a run, not a new breakout. We sell into it.
wrong.Nothing, let the trail decide: The trail is slow. In a climax it gives back a lot. Sell a big part into strength.

questions.answer: Sell a big part into the run
questions.why: Sell a big part into it. Three up days, two overnight gap ups, range and volume expanding. That's a parabolic burst. A burst is a short final leg of 3 to 5 days, and final legs are where runs end. Buyers are paying anything right now, and they're who you sell to. How much is your call, but I want a big piece off while it's there. The trail handles the rest.
questions.lesson_line: A climax run is a gift. Sell a big part into it.
questions.simple: Sell a big part. A burst like this is often the last leg of a run, so sell to the buyers paying up.

deeper.trap: Not every strong run is a climax. A burst is a 3 to 5 day final leg. It checks several boxes: up days, overnight gap ups, range expansion and rising volume. One big day isn't it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook C34, a judgment call
how big a 'big part' is stays the owner's judgment

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: We buy leaders: an RS rating of ___ or more, in one of the strongest groups.
questions.why: 80. Our rulebook buys leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups. The exceptions are parabolic and mean-reversion trades.
questions.lesson_line: Buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in a strong group.
questions.simple: We buy leaders, so the stock needs an RS rating of 80 or more and a place in one of the strongest groups.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook C31
the cutoff of 80 is a rule that could be retuned

questions.q: Which one do you buy?
questions.story: Two clean cups trigger the same morning. One stock has an RS rating of 92 in a top group. The other has a rating of 55 in a weak group.
choices: The 92 in the strong group
The 55, it has more room
Both, at half size
Neither, skip both today

wrong.The 55, it has more room: A 55 in a weak group is a laggard. We buy leaders, 80 or more.
wrong.Both, at half size: Half size doesn't turn a laggard into a leader. Take the 92.
wrong.Neither, skip both today: The 92 passes the leader test and the chart is clean. That one's a buy.

questions.why: The 92. We buy leaders, an RS rating of 80 or more in one of the strongest groups. A 92 means it's been beating most of the market, and a strong group gives it a tailwind. The 55 in a weak group is a laggard with a clean chart. When the market pushes, leaders go first. Check the RS rating in our app before you buy.
questions.lesson_line: A clean chart on a laggard is still a laggard. Buy the leader.
questions.simple: The 92. Leaders beat most of the market and lead the next push, and a 55 in a weak group lags.

deeper.trap: Both charts look clean, so shape can't separate them. The leader test can. The only exceptions are parabolic and mean-reversion trades, and a cup is neither.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook C31

questions.q: Great numbers. Do you buy the breakout?
questions.story: A stock grows sales and earnings every quarter. Its cup is a sharp V, with a 5-day dip at the rim. Price trades through the handle high.
choices: Pass, the chart comes first
Pass, the handle is too short
Buy, the growth beats the shape
Buy half size and trim fast

wrong.Buy half size and trim fast: Small size doesn't fix a bad shape. Wait for a real base.
wrong.Pass, the handle is too short: Five days is long enough for a handle. The V cup is the problem.
wrong.Buy, the growth beats the shape: Growth is a plus, but the chart decides first, and a V fails it.

questions.why: Pass. I love growing sales and earnings, and it's a big plus. But the chart comes first, because it shows what buyers are doing right now. This cup is a V, straight down and straight back up, with no rest at the bottom. V shapes are less reliable. Great numbers will still be great numbers when it builds a real base.
questions.lesson_line: Growth is a plus. The chart decides first.
questions.simple: Pass. Growth is a plus, but the chart shows what buyers do now, and a V cup fails the chart.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook D40

questions.q: A perfect-looking cup is still a buy when the stock trades under its 200-day.
questions.why: False. Under the 200-day we don't buy stocks, period. That line is the average of the last 200 sessions. Below it, the long trend is down, and every rally runs into holders who want out. A pretty cup doesn't change who's sitting above it. The only exception is indexes and the double or triple ETFs, on a reversal extension or a parabolic long. Never a single stock.
questions.lesson_line: No long under the 200-day. A tidy cup doesn't change that.
questions.simple: False. Under the 200-day the long trend is down, so we don't buy the stock, however clean the cup.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B26

questions.q: Clean cup, and it's trading through the 31.40 pivot. The 200-day is up at 33.10. Which check decides this trade?
choices: It's under the 200-day
It's chasing past 4%
Earnings are too close
It's stretched over the 9 EMA

wrong.It's chasing past 4%: It's right at the pivot, so there's no chase. The 200-day is what decides.
wrong.Earnings are too close: Nothing here says a report is coming. The 200-day decides it.
wrong.It's stretched over the 9 EMA: Nothing says it's stretched, and it's right at the pivot. The 200-day decides it.

questions.why: It's under the 200-day. The pivot is 31.40 and the 200-day sits at 33.10, so price is below it. For a stock that's a hard no, however clean the cup. I check the 200-day before I even look at the pivot. If it fails that, nothing else matters.
questions.lesson_line: Check the 200-day before the pivot. Under it, no long.
questions.simple: Price is under its 200-day, so the long trend is down, and we don't buy the stock.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B26

questions.q: This cup looks great. It trades 600,000 shares a day at $28. How much money changes hands a day?
questions.why: 16.8 million dollars a day. Price times shares, $28 times 600,000. That's under our $20 million floor, so I skip it, however clean the cup. Thin names are easy to buy and hard to sell. When you need out, there's nobody on the other side and you give up a chunk just to exit. We trade stocks at $10 or more that do at least $20 million a day.
questions.lesson_line: Price times shares is dollars traded. We want $20 million a day.
questions.simple: It trades 16.8 million dollars a day, under the 20 million floor, so getting out would be hard.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (B23)

choices: $1.7 million
$0.6 million
$16.8 million
$168 million

wrong.$0.6 million: That's the share count in millions. Multiply by the $28 price.
wrong.$168 million: Decimal slip. 600,000 times $28 is a bit under 17 million.
wrong.$1.7 million: Decimal slip the other way. It's 16.8 million.

questions.q: A $7 stock that trades $40 million a day is liquid enough for us to buy.
questions.why: False. We want $10 a share and $20 million a day, and both have to pass. This one clears the dollars at $40 million, but it fails the price. The dollar line is what gets you in and out. The price line keeps us in the kind of stocks we actually trade. Skip it and find a name that passes both.
questions.lesson_line: Both count: $10 a share and $20 million a day.
questions.simple: False. Both lines have to pass, and a $7 stock fails the $10 minimum, whatever it trades.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B23

questions.q: This cup trades 250,000 shares a day. How many shares is the most you'd own?
questions.why: 2,500 shares. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and 1% of 250,000 is 2,500. The reason is the exit. Own a big slice of a day's volume and selling it moves the price against you. The worse the day, the worse your fill. At 1% or less you can get out without being the whole market. That cap holds whatever the risk math says.
questions.lesson_line: Cap every position at 1% of average daily volume.
questions.simple: 2,500 shares, 1% of a day's volume, so you can get out without moving the price.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (D42)

choices: 2,500 shares
25,000 shares
250,000 shares
125,000 shares

wrong.25,000 shares: That's ten percent of the volume, a decimal slip.
wrong.250,000 shares: That's the whole day's volume, not the cap.
wrong.125,000 shares: That's half the day's volume. The cap is one percent.

questions.q: How many shares do you buy?
questions.story: The risk math and the position cap allow 5,000 shares of a cup breakout. The stock averages 220,000 shares a day. You hold none today.
choices: 2,200 shares
3,600 shares
220 shares
1,100 shares

wrong.3,600 shares: Averaging the two limits isn't a rule, and it's still over 1% of the day's volume.
wrong.1,100 shares: That's half the cap. The most you can buy is the cap itself.
wrong.220 shares: Decimal slip, a tenth of the cap.

questions.why: 2,200 shares. The risk math says 5,000, but this stock only trades 220,000 shares a day. We never own more than 1% of that, which is 2,200. Size is always the smallest of your limits. Own more than 1% and getting out on a bad day means pushing the price down on yourself.
questions.lesson_line: Whatever the risk math says, never own more than 1% of a day's volume.
questions.simple: 2,200 shares, 1% of a day's volume. The smaller limit wins so you can still get out cleanly.

deeper.trap: The cap counts what you own, not one order. Buying the cap now and the same again later leaves double the cap held. Averaging the two limits gives 3,600, still over the cap.

reasons: a computed key (220,000 / 100)
rests on the owner's rulebook D42; the story says the risk math and the position cap allow 5,000, so the volume cap is the only extra limit

questions.q: On our card, the down weeks on a cup's left side roughly match the up weeks on its right side.
questions.why: True. IBD says the number of down weeks on the left side should roughly match the number of up weeks on the right side. Our card uses the same cue. The match is rough, not exact. A lopsided cup grades down.
questions.lesson_line: A good cup is symmetric: weeks down on the left, weeks up on the right.
questions.simple: True. A good cup is balanced, with the weeks down on the left roughly equal to the weeks up on the right.

reasons: the symmetry cue is a card cue with IBD as the main source

questions.q: A cup slides down for 8 weeks, then snaps back to the high in 2. How do you grade that shape?
choices: Lopsided, so it grades lower
Lopsided, but same grade
Strong, a fast climb is best
Fine, if the handle dries up

wrong.Fine, if the handle dries up: A quiet handle is a separate plus. It doesn't fix a lopsided cup.
wrong.Lopsided, but same grade: Lopsided is right, but it's less clean, so it grades lower.
wrong.Strong, a fast climb is best: A fast snap back isn't the goal. I want the right side to take about as long as the left.

questions.why: Lopsided, and I'd grade it lower. A good cup is roughly even, about as many weeks coming back as it took going down. Eight weeks down and two up is a slow slide and a snap back. The stock never rebuilt on the right side, so holders trapped up top haven't had time to leave. It's not a no. It's a less clean setup, so it gets less size.
questions.lesson_line: Count the weeks down and the weeks up. I want them roughly even.
questions.simple: Lopsided. A slow slide and a quick snap back never rebuilt the right side, so it's less clean.

reasons: the symmetry cue is a card cue with IBD as the main source

deeper.example: IBD: the number of down weeks on the left side should roughly match the number of up weeks on the right side.

questions.q: A typical handle forms over about one to four weeks.
questions.why: True. AAII says a handle typically forms over about one to four weeks. StockCharts says it is ideally completed within one to four weeks, though a handle can last longer. Our card says usually 1 to 4 weeks, and grades one over about 22 sessions down.
questions.lesson_line: A typical handle runs one to four weeks.
questions.simple: True. A typical handle takes about one to four weeks, and AAII and StockCharts agree.

reasons: the 22-session grading line is a card proposal
AAII also says longer handles can signal bigger moves, so sources are not fully aligned

questions.q: What does our card do with it?
questions.story: A cup has a quiet handle. Its lows drift down and every close holds above the 50-day. It has now run 24 sessions with no breakout.
choices: Grade it down; keep it listed
Drop it; the handle is stale
Grade it up; a long handle is best
Buy now, before it gets older

wrong.Drop it; the handle is stale: Stale starts past about 30 sessions. This handle is at 24.
wrong.Grade it up; a long handle is best: Long handles grade down. A typical handle runs 1 to 4 weeks.
wrong.Buy now, before it gets older: The buy is the trade through the handle high. No trade, no buy.

questions.answer: Grade it down; keep it listed
questions.why: Grade it down; keep it on the list. The card grades a handle over about 22 sessions down, and this one is at 24. It goes stale, and comes off, only past about 30 sessions with no breakout. The falling lows and the 50-day hold are what a good handle shows, so it stays on the list.
questions.lesson_line: Handles over about 22 sessions grade down. Past about 30 they are stale.
questions.simple: A handle over about 22 sessions is graded down. It is stale only past about 30 sessions, and this one is at 24.

deeper.trap: Two different lines. About 22 sessions is where the grade drops. About 30 sessions is where the card takes the setup off. In between it is still live, only graded lower. Neither line is a buy signal: the buy is still the trade through the handle high.

reasons: the 22 and 30 session lines are card proposals
AAII's remark that longer handles can signal bigger moves differs from the card's grade-down rule

questions.q: Handle high 50.00, handle low 47.50. How deep is the handle, in percent?
questions.why: 5.0%. The fall is 50.00 minus 47.50, which is 2.50. Divided by the handle's own high, 50.00, that is 5.0%. Our card calls a handle of 8% or less better, and about 5% best. Zanger's 5% is measured from the old high point, which is a different yardstick.
questions.lesson_line: Handle depth is the fall from its own high. Shallower grades higher.
questions.simple: Depth is the fall from the handle's own high as a percent, and here that is 5.0%.

reasons: a computed key
the 8% and 5% grade cues are card numbers

wrong.2.5%: Read the dollar drop as a percent.
wrong.0.5%: Decimal slip: moved the decimal one place left.
wrong.2.6%: Divided the drop by the high plus the low, not the high.

questions.q: Which handle grades highest on our card?
questions.story: Three clean cups, each with a quiet handle that drifts down. The handles are 5%, 7% and 11% deep.
choices: The 5% deep handle
The 7% handle
The 11% handle
They grade alike

wrong.They grade alike: Depth counts on our card: 8% or less is better, and about 5% is best.
wrong.The 7% handle: Good, since 8% or less is better, but about 5% is best.
wrong.The 11% handle: 11% is past 8%, so it grades lower. A deeper handle gives back more.

questions.why: The 5% handle. Our card grades a handle of 8% or less better, and about 5% best. The 7% handle is under 8%, so it is good but not best. The 11% handle is past 8%, so it grades lower. IBD says a handle's secondary decline is usually no more than 8% to 12%. So 11% is a lower grade, not a different pattern.
questions.lesson_line: Handles of 8% or less grade better. About 5% is best.
questions.simple: The 5% handle grades highest. Our card likes 8% or less, and about 5% is best.

deeper.trap: Do not read 'grades highest' as 'the others fail'. All three handles can be valid. The card prefers 8% or less and about 5% best, and IBD's usual range for a handle's dip runs up to about 8% to 12%. The 11% handle simply earns a lower grade.

reasons: the 8% and 5% cues are card numbers that may be retuned
close to the pending handle-depth decision D-053 but not keyed on it

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: IBD says a handle should generally form ___ the 50-day or 10-week moving average.
questions.why: Above. IBD says a handle should generally form above the 50-day or 10-week moving averages. Our card is stricter: a close below the 50-day during the handle ends the setup before the buy.
questions.lesson_line: A good handle holds above the 50-day.
questions.simple: A handle should generally sit above the 50-day line, and our card wants no close under it.

reasons: the card's one-close test is stricter than IBD's 'generally', a card proposal

questions.q: Is that a good plan?
questions.story: You bought a cup breakout at 54.57 with the stop at 52.94. You plan to watch the screen and sell by hand if it breaks 52.94.
choices: No, put in a real stop order
Fine, if you stay at the screen
Fine, the stop is tight
Set an alert and sell by hand

wrong.Fine, if you stay at the screen: You can't watch every second, and a stop kept in your head isn't a stop.
wrong.Fine, the stop is tight: A tight stop doesn't make a mental one safe. The order goes in with your broker.
wrong.Set an alert and sell by hand: An alert is a reminder, not an order. Every position gets a real stop order.

questions.answer: No, put in a real stop order
questions.why: No. Put the stop in as a real order with your broker. A stop in your head only works if you're at the screen at the exact moment, and you won't always be. You'll be on a call, at lunch, or watching another name. And when it gets there, you'll hesitate and hope. A real order takes the decision out of the moment. Set it right after you buy, then only move it up.
questions.lesson_line: A stop in your head isn't a stop. Put the order in.
questions.simple: No. Put the stop in as a real order, because a stop in your head only works when you're watching.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook D41

questions.q: Once you're in, the stop only moves up, never down, except after a gap through it.
questions.why: True. The stop is where the trade is proven wrong, and you set it before you bought. Moving it down after the fact turns a small planned loss into a bigger one. That's how accounts bleed. The one exception is a gap through the stop. Then the low of the first 30-minute bar becomes the new stop, with 2R as the ceiling.
questions.lesson_line: The stop only moves up. A gap through it is the one exception.
questions.simple: True. Lowering the stop turns a small loss into a bigger one, and a gap through your stop is the only exception.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook A4 and D41

questions.q: What do you do at the open?
questions.story: You bought at 91.29 with the stop at 90.67, so 3R is 93.15. On day 4 it gaps open at 94.20, above that mark.
choices: Sell part, it's the rule
Wait for a dip to 93.15
Sell two thirds right away
Your call, sell part or hold

wrong.Sell part, it's the rule: Selling part into a gap is a choice you can make. It's never a rule.
wrong.Wait for a dip to 93.15: No rule asks for a dip. Waiting is a bet that it comes back.
wrong.Sell two thirds right away: Too much at once. If you sell, sell part and keep the rest working.

questions.answer: Your call, sell part or hold
questions.why: It's your call. A gap past 3R isn't an automatic sell. Selling part at the open banks money while buyers are paying up. Holding keeps the whole position on a stock that's clearly strong. It's day 4, past the day 3 mark where I start thinking about a first sell. Selling some into a big gap is one choice I make, but it's judgment, never a rule.
questions.lesson_line: A gap past your sell level isn't an order to sell. It's your call.
questions.simple: Your call. A gap past 3R isn't an automatic sell, and selling part or holding are both fair.

deeper.trap: Do not read the gap as an order to sell. 93.15 is a mark, not a trigger. The gap lets you sell part by judgment. It does not make you.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B19 and F63

questions.q: If a stock opens above 3R, we wait for it to fall back to 3R before we trim.
questions.why: False. The rule is that if a stock opens above a trim level (3R or 5R), we take that trim at the open. Waiting for a pullback to 3R is a bet that the pullback comes, and the rule does not make that bet.
questions.lesson_line: Opens above a trim level: take that trim at the open.
questions.simple: False. When a stock opens above a trim level, we take the trim at the open and do not wait for a pullback.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook F63

questions.q: Before the buy, a quiet handle is still off the list if its midpoint sits below the cup's midpoint.
questions.why: True. Our card ends the setup before the buy if the handle's midpoint sits below the cup's midpoint. IBD wants the handle's midpoint above the cup's midpoint, and says handles that form too low present added risk of failure. Quiet volume does not make up for a handle that is too low.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet is not enough. The handle must sit above the cup's midpoint.
questions.simple: True. A handle must sit above the middle of the cup, and a handle that sits lower is too low to buy.

reasons: the card's midpoint test is a proposal with IBD behind it

questions.q: Read those lows. What kind of handle is this?
questions.story: A clean cup, then a 6-session handle. Its lows run 47.0, 47.2, 47.4, 47.6, 47.9 and 48.3. Volume dries up.
choices: A wedging handle, it often fails
A tight handle, the best kind
A short handle, it doesn't count
A flat handle, it passes

wrong.A tight handle, the best kind: Tight closes are a different cue. These lows climb, so you're looking at a wedge.
wrong.A short handle, it doesn't count: Six sessions is long enough. The rising lows are the problem.
wrong.A flat handle, it passes: Flat lows would pass, but these climb from 47.0 to 48.3.

questions.answer: A wedging handle, it often fails
questions.why: A wedge. The lows climb every session, 47.0 up to 48.3. A good handle drifts sideways to down and shakes out weak holders by undercutting a prior low. This one never does. Everyone who bought the climb is still in, waiting to sell the first pop. The dried-up volume is nice, but it doesn't fix the slope. Wedging handles fail more often, so I pass.
questions.lesson_line: Read the handle's lows. Rising lows are a wedge, and I pass.
questions.simple: A wedge. The lows climb every day with no shakeout, and wedging handles fail more often.

deeper.trap: Dried-up volume isn't proof of a good handle. Volume is one cue and the slope of the lows is another. IBD: a wedging handle with no shakeouts is a sign to steer clear.

reasons: the slope test is a card proposal with IBD behind it

questions.q: A 4-session dip under the rim becomes a handle if the breakout comes on heavy volume.
questions.why: False. IBD says if it's shorter than five days, it's not a handle. Our card also needs a handle of at least 5 sessions, and a shorter one ends the setup before the buy. Breakout volume is a separate cue and does not change the count of a 4-session dip.
questions.lesson_line: Under five sessions is not a handle, whatever the volume.
questions.simple: False. A dip shorter than five days is not a handle, so heavy breakout volume cannot rescue it.

deeper.trap: Do not let a strong breakout argue the setup into shape. Count the sessions first: at least 5. A named mistake on the card is calling a 2 or 3-day dip a handle, and a 4-day dip is only a little longer.

reasons: IBD and the card agree on the 5-session minimum

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: We skip a long that is more than ___ percent above its 10-day average.
questions.why: 10. Our rulebook skips a long that is more than 10% above its 10-day average, because it is too stretched to buy. The 4% line is a different test: how far past the buy point you may pay.
questions.lesson_line: More than 10% above the 10-day is too stretched. Skip it.
questions.simple: A long more than 10% above its 10-day average is too stretched to buy.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C29, settled)
added so the stretch rule is taught before q43 applies it

questions.q: Your stock gaps down through your stop. If the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, you get out right away.
questions.why: True. After a gap through your stop, the low of the first 30-minute bar becomes the new stop. That gives the stock a chance to find its real low instead of selling into the opening panic. But there's a ceiling. If those 30 minutes push the loss past 2R, twice what you planned to risk, you're out. A gap should never cost you more than that.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop has a ceiling. Past 2R in the first 30 minutes, you're out.
questions.simple: True. Past 2R in the first 30 minutes we get out, so a gap can't cost more than that.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20, the gap rule and its 2R ceiling)
added so the gap rule and its ceiling are taught before q32 applies them

questions.story: You bought the cup breakout at 48.60. The low of the day is 46.40, about 4.5% under your fill.
questions.q: Your normal size doesn't fit that stop. What do you do?
choices: Fewer shares, stop stays at the low
Move the stop up so the size fits
Full size, it's only one trade
Keep the stop, round the size up
questions.answer: Fewer shares, stop stays at the low

wrong.Move the stop up so the size fits: That puts the stop inside the day's normal noise. The size follows the stop, never the reverse.
wrong.Full size, it's only one trade: Full size at a 4.5% stop means risking more than you planned. The stop sets the size.
wrong.Keep the stop, round the size up: Shares get rounded down, never up, so a stop-out never costs more than you chose.

questions.simple: Fewer shares. The stop goes where the chart says you're wrong, and the size comes from the stop.
questions.why: Fewer shares. Your stop goes a few cents under 46.40, the low of the day. That's where the chart says you're wrong. About 4.5% is wider than I like, but under 5% I'll take it. The size comes from the stop, never the other way around. Pull the stop up just to fit more shares and normal noise takes you out of a good trade. So you buy fewer shares, or you wait for a tighter entry.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, size second. Never the other way around.

deeper.trap: The trap is pulling the stop in to get the size you wanted. Start from the honest stop, a few cents under the low of the day, and take the size it gives. If that doesn't fit your risk, skip the trade.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook A3 and A5
no percent is keyed, so the pending stop-width decision is not leaned on

questions.q: What's that volume telling you?
questions.story: A rounded 10-week cup falls 20%, then a handle forms in its upper half. The handle drifts down for eight sessions above the 50-day. Volume rises every session, and the handle's average tops the cup's.
choices: A warning, it grades lower
Pass, loud volume voids it
Buy, rising volume is demand
Pass, eight sessions is short

wrong.Pass, loud volume voids it: Volume raises or lowers the grade. It doesn't void a setup.
wrong.Buy, rising volume is demand: In a handle, rising volume means sellers are still active. A handle should dry up.
wrong.Pass, eight sessions is short: Eight sessions is long enough. The shape and the 50-day hold are fine.

questions.why: It's a warning, and I'd grade it lower. A handle should get quiet as the last sellers leave. Here volume climbs every session and tops the cup's average. That says sellers are still feeding stock into every bounce. It doesn't kill the setup, since volume only raises or lowers the grade. But it's less clean, so it gets less size, and I watch the breakout closely.
questions.lesson_line: A handle should dry up. Volume that climbs through it is a warning and a lower grade.
questions.simple: A warning. Rising volume says sellers are still around, so it grades lower, but it doesn't kill the setup.

reasons: the volume gate is a proposed card row, not an owner ruling
IBD gives the direction of handle volume, no number
the story fails both readings of the row: a rising trend and an average above the cup's

deeper.example: IBD: volume should dry up, evidence that the weak holders are just about gone. Volume should mostly ease until the breakout.

questions.q: A rounded base took 5 weeks to form, handle included. Does it count as a cup with handle on our card?
choices: No. It is under our 7-week minimum
Yes. A rounded shape is all it needs
Yes, if the handle is quiet enough
No. A cup needs at least 12 weeks
questions.answer: No. It is under our 7-week minimum
questions.why: No. Our card wants a cup with handle at least 7 weeks long, handle included. That is 35 sessions from the left-side high to the day before the breakout. IBD asks for seven weeks too. A 5-week base has not had time to build a cup.
questions.lesson_line: Seven weeks or more. A real cup takes time to build.

wrong.Yes. A rounded shape is all it needs: Shape is not enough. The card also wants at least 7 weeks, handle included.
wrong.Yes, if the handle is quiet enough: A quiet handle helps the grade. It does not make up for a base under 7 weeks.
wrong.No. A cup needs at least 12 weeks: Too long. The minimum is 7 weeks, not 12. Bulkowski's range starts at 7 too.

questions.simple: A cup with handle must run at least 7 weeks, handle included, so a 5-week base is too short.

reasons: IBD and Bulkowski agree

questions.q: Does the handle pass the card's 50-day test?
questions.story: The handle is eight sessions old and its 50-day line sits at 61.40. On day five the stock trades down to 61.10, then closes at 62.30. Every other close is above the line too.
choices: Yes; no close was under the 50-day
No; the intraday low went under it
No; it needs a close over the 20 EMA
Yes; but only on light volume
questions.answer: Yes; no close was under the 50-day
questions.why: Yes. On our card the handle holds above the 50-day when no daily close is below it. The dip to 61.10 was intraday, and every close, including 62.30, stayed above the line at 61.40. IBD says a handle should generally form above the 50-day. A close under the line would end the setup before the buy.
questions.lesson_line: The 50-day test counts closes. A low that dips under and closes back above still passes.
questions.simple: Yes. The card counts closes, and every close in the handle stayed above the 50-day line.

wrong.No; the intraday low went under it: The card's test is the daily close. A low under the line that closes back above it does not end the handle. A close under the line would.
wrong.Yes; but only on light volume: Volume is its own test: the handle should average quieter than the cup. It does not change the 50-day test, which looks only at closes.
wrong.No; it needs a close over the 20 EMA: The card names the 50-day for the handle. It does not ask for the 20 EMA.

questions.q: 19 days is a long handle. Is it still one you'd buy?
questions.story: A leader ran 40%, then built a 21.6-week, 21.3% deep cup. The handle has now run 19 days and is 6.7% deep. Its lows drift down and its volume is 0.77x the cup's.
choices: Yes, lows drift down, volume dries up
No, a handle must be under two weeks
No, this long means a stale base
Yes, a longer handle is stronger
questions.answer: Yes, lows drift down, volume dries up

wrong.No, a handle must be under two weeks: There's no two-week cap. A handle can run a few weeks and still work.
wrong.No, this long means a stale base: Stale is a handle that drags on with no drift and no breakout. This one still drifts down and dries up.
wrong.Yes, a longer handle is stronger: Length isn't the strength. How it behaves is.

questions.why: Yes. I judge a handle by how it acts more than by how long it runs. This one's lows drift down, so it's shaking out weak holders. Volume is 0.77x the cup's, so the sellers are drying up. 19 days is long, but it's still a quiet drift, not a stall. It went on to hit 3R in 4 sessions.
questions.lesson_line: Judge a handle by how it acts, not just how long it runs.
questions.simple: Yes. Its lows drift down and volume dries up, and that matters more than how long it runs.

reasons: new in review7 (replaces the cut handle-length items)

deeper.counter: StockCharts: the handle can last from one week to many weeks and is ideally completed within one to four weeks. AAII says about one to four weeks too.

questions.q: A cup climbs back to its old high, then dips into a handle. What's going on in that dip?
choices: Holders near the old high are selling
The stock is failing and rolling over
Funds have finished buying the stock
The cup's low is being retested
questions.answer: Holders near the old high are selling

wrong.The stock is failing and rolling over: A handle that holds in the top half is a pause, not a failure. The selling is getting worked off.
wrong.Funds have finished buying the stock: Nothing on the chart says that. The dip is the old-high selling getting worked off.
wrong.The cup's low is being retested: A handle forms in the top half of the base. A fall back to the cup's low is a broken base, not a handle.

questions.why: Holders near the old high are selling. Some bought up there and sat through the whole cup underwater. Now they're back near even and want out. Others just get scared. The handle is where that supply gets worked off. Once those holders are gone, there's less selling left to stop a breakout. That's why we wait for the trade through the handle's high.
questions.lesson_line: The handle is the old-high selling getting worked off. Wait for the trade through its high.
questions.simple: Holders near the old high are selling to get out. Once they're gone, less is left to stop the breakout.

reasons: new in review7 (the why of the handle, from Zanger and IBD)

deeper.counter: Zanger: as the stock comes up to test the old highs, the stock will incur selling pressure. IBD: a shakeout in the handle serves to scare out weak hands, shareholders who lack conviction.
